Rules for today

  1. Answer the guiding question in every paragraph.
  2. Quote briefly: three to six words, embedded in your own sentence.
  3. After every quotation, name the technique, explain its effect on the listener and link it to purpose. This is the golden chain: technique, quotation, effect, purpose.
  4. If you run out of time on a step, write a one-line note of what you would say and move on.
  5. Work on your own. Do not use AI.

Minutes 13 to 25 · Step 2

The introduction

A strong introduction does four jobs in four to six sentences: it sets the context, identifies the text, states its central message and gives a thesis that answers the guiding question.

MoveWhat it doesLength
1. FrameA general claim about the topic or text type1 sentence
2. IdentifyTitle, speakers or producer, text type, date, platform, audience1 to 2 sentences
3. MessageWhat the text says and what it wants the listener to do or feel1 sentence
4. ThesisYour argument about HOW the text achieves its purpose, naming your three focuses1 sentence

Useful vocabulary: podcast transcript, edited extract, host, guest, expert testimony, ethos, logos, pathos, conversational register, anecdote, extended metaphor, implied audience, call to action.

Checkpoint, minute 25: move on to body paragraph 1.

Minutes 79 to 87 · Step 6

The conclusion

A conclusion restates your thesis in fresh words, draws your three paragraphs into one insight and ends on a final thought about significance. It adds no new evidence.

  1. Restate: your thesis, reworded.
  2. Synthesise: one sentence that pulls your three focuses together.
  3. Widen: what the text reveals about its audience, its context or the way texts persuade.
Sentence starters
  • In conclusion, the text presents [topic] as...
  • Together, [focus 1], [focus 2] and [focus 3] show that...
  • Tellingly, the text ends with..., which suggests...
  • Ultimately, the text reveals how [text type]s persuade their audience by...
